case_analysis.focal_point: Whether PROMESA § 106(a)’s directive that actions against the Financial Oversight and Management Board for Puerto Rico “shall be brought” in a U.S. district court clearly and unmistakably abrogates any sovereign immunity the Board may assert against federal and territorial claims.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Puerto Rico Oversight, Management, and Economic Stability Act (PROMESA) § 106(a), 48 U.S.C. § 2126(a) (and, in the background, Puerto Rico Constitution art. II, § 4; and the doctrine of state/territorial sovereign immunity as analogized to Eleventh Amendment immunity principles).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: The Board argues it is immune from suit (as an arm of Puerto Rico and/or by statutory protections) and that PROMESA § 106(a) is merely a forum-selection/jurisdiction-channeling provision that specifies where suits must be filed if otherwise permitted; it does not contain the clear statement required to abrogate sovereign immunity, so the CPI disclosure action cannot proceed absent an explicit waiver/abrogation.
case_analysis.respondent_position: CPI argues Puerto Rico may not enjoy state-like sovereign immunity (or, if it does, the Board should not benefit from it), and in any event Congress—acting under the Territory Clause—abrogated any immunity the Board might claim through PROMESA § 106(a) by mandating that actions against the Board be brought in federal district court, which CPI contends necessarily authorizes such suits (including territorial-law access-to-information claims).
key_precedents: Leopold v. CIA (D.C. Cir.) (interlocutory appealability of certain disclosure-related orders characterized as injunctive)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor is right to stress PROMESA’s comprehensive accountability design and Congress’s Territory Clause authority, and § 106(a)’s focus on “any action against the Oversight Board” is more tailored than an ordinary jurisdictional grant. But as Justice Kagan and Justice Thomas emphasize, our clear-statement precedents (Atascadero, Dellmuth, Lane, Sossamon) require unmistakable textual displacement of immunity, and mandatory forum language—without “may be sued,” “waives,” or “shall not be immune”—is the paradigm of what those cases deem insufficient. Justice Alito’s point that § 106(a) is not paired with an express cause of action and remedial scheme that would be frustrated absent abrogation reinforces the minimal, legitimacy-preserving reading: § 106(a) channels where otherwise-permitted suits must be filed, without itself creating or enlarging suability. I would keep the holding narrow, leaving open whether some other PROMESA provision, or an express waiver, could authorize suit in a different case.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s contextual claim—that PROMESA’s purpose and Puerto Rico’s territorial status make § 106(a) an affirmative authorization of suit—still cannot overcome the clear-statement rule, which is grounded in the statutory text and requires unmistakable language to strip immunity. As the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan emphasize, § 106(a) reads as classic forum-channeling (“shall be brought” in a specified court) and, under Atascadero, Dellmuth, and Lane v. Peña, such jurisdictional/venue directives do not themselves abrogate sovereign immunity. Justice Alito’s point that § 106(a) is not paired with an express cause of action or remedial scheme reinforces that we should not transform a routing clause into a sweeping waiver by inference. Whatever Congress’s Territory Clause power, it must be exercised through clear words if immunity is to be displaced, and those words are absent here.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s contextual point about PROMESA’s accountability structure and Congress’s Territory Clause power does not overcome the clear-statement rule: as Justice Kagan and the Chief Justice emphasize, § 106(a) reads like classic forum-channeling language and never uses the unmistakable vocabulary (“may be sued,” “not immune,” “abrogated”) our cases demand. Precedents like Atascadero, Dellmuth, Lane, and Sossamon treat jurisdictional/venue directives as insufficient precisely because they require an inference from purpose and structure to immunity-stripping—an inference we have repeatedly rejected. Justice Roberts’s observation that § 106(a) is not paired with an express cause of action and tailored remedial scheme underscores the practical problem: converting a routing clause into a sweeping waiver would invite broad, fiscally consequential litigation without a clearly specified remedial design. I therefore continue to read § 106(a) as specifying the exclusive forum for suits otherwise authorized, not as itself abrogating any immunity the Board may enjoy.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The Chief Justice and Justice Kagan press the clear-statement line—Atascadero, Lane, and Sossamon caution that jurisdictional or forum language is usually not enough to displace immunity—and I take that concern seriously. But § 106(a) is not a generic jurisdictional grant; it is a targeted command that "any action against the Oversight Board" shall be brought in a particular federal court, and that specificity, in PROMESA’s integrated oversight-and-accountability design, reads as Congress affirmatively contemplating suits against the Board rather than merely routing hypothetical suits that may never exist. Justice Alito’s Seminole Tribe-style “no cause of action/remedy pairing” point does not defeat that reading here because PROMESA’s structure relies on judicial review to cabin an entity exercising sweeping territorial power, and insulating it would have severe, real-world access-to-justice consequences for Puerto Rico’s residents. Under my pragmatic approach, context matters in determining whether Congress spoke clearly enough: in this statute, Congress’s explicit focus on actions “against the Board” and the exclusivity of the federal forum provide the requisite clarity even if the statute lacks the usual immunity vocabulary.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s best argument remains that § 106(a)’s directive that actions “shall be brought” in federal court, targeted to “any action against the Oversight Board,” fits PROMESA’s accountability design and Congress’s Territory Clause power. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Thomas emphasize, our clear-statement rule is a textual interpretive constraint: forum-channeling language—even mandatory and specific—does not unmistakably speak to waiver/abrogation, and purpose/context cannot supply the missing “not immune/may be sued” signal (Atascadero, Lane, Sossamon). Justice Alito’s point about the absence of an express cause of action/remedial pairing reinforces the practical and doctrinal hazard of converting a routing clause into a broad authorization to sue on territorial-law claims. I therefore continue to read § 106(a) as specifying the exclusive forum for suits otherwise permitted, not as itself stripping any immunity the Board may have.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s accountability-and-context argument has force as a matter of policy, but it cannot overcome the clear-statement rule: § 106(a)’s “shall be brought” language reads as forum-channeling, not an unequivocal waiver/abrogation, and our cases (as the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan emphasize) refuse to treat jurisdictional or routing clauses as immunity-stripping. Justice Alito’s point that § 106(a) is not paired with a distinct cause of action and remedial scheme underscores why we should not convert a venue directive into a sweeping authorization to hale an allegedly immune entity into court on territorial-law claims. Puerto Rico’s territorial status may affect the source or scope of the Board’s immunity, but, as Justice Thomas notes, it does not relax the interpretive requirement that Congress speak unmistakably in the statutory text when it means to displace immunity. I therefore remain convinced § 106(a) specifies where otherwise-permitted suits must be filed, not that it silently creates new suits against an immune defendant.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s accountability-focused reading of § 106(a)—that “any action against the Oversight Board … shall be brought” in federal court functions as affirmative authorization—raises a serious practical concern about insulating a powerful entity from judicial checks. John Roberts.reasoning: PROMESA § 106(a) is best read as a jurisdiction-channeling provision—specifying the exclusive forum for suits that are otherwise authorized—rather than an unequivocal congressional abrogation of sovereign immunity. Under Atascadero State Hosp. v. Scanlon and Dellmuth v. Muth, Congress must make its intent to abrogate immunity “unmistakably clear in the language of the statute,” and “shall be brought” language that merely directs where actions are filed does not satisfy that clear-statement rule. Nothing in § 106(a) expressly subjects the Board to suit or removes any immunity it may possess, and a narrow construction avoids unnecessary disruption to institutional legitimacy while respecting federalism and precedent. Accordingly, absent a clearer abrogation or waiver elsewhere in PROMESA, the Board may assert immunity against these claims.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: PROMESA § 106(a), 48 U.S.C. § 2126(a), is textually a jurisdiction/channeling provision—directing where suits "shall be brought"—and it nowhere mentions immunity, waiver, or abrogation. Under this Court’s clear-statement rule, Congress must make any intent to abrogate sovereign immunity “unmistakably clear,” and courts may not supply that intent through inference from statutory structure or purpose. Lane v. Pena, 518 U.S. 187, 192 (1996), and Dellmuth v. Muth, 491 U.S. 223, 228–232 (1989), require an unequivocal textual expression, which § 106(a) lacks. Because the statute does not clearly abrogate whatever sovereign immunity the Board may possess, the suit cannot proceed absent an explicit waiver or abrogation.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: PROMESA § 106(a) is, on its face, a forum-selection and jurisdiction-channeling provision—directing where an action "shall be brought"—and it contains no express reference to sovereign immunity or to an abrogation of it. Under the clear-statement rule, a jurisdictional grant alone does not "clearly and unmistakably" abrogate sovereign immunity. See Atascadero State Hosp. v. Scanlon, 473 U.S. 234, 246 (1985), and Blatchford v. Native Vill. of Noatak, 501 U.S. 775, 786 n.4 (1991). Unlike Seminole Tribe v. Florida, 517 U.S. 44, 56–57 (1996), PROMESA does not pair § 106(a) with a specific cause of action and remedial scheme against the Board that would be thwarted absent abrogation, so practical consequences counsel against reading an “unprecedented” abrogation into a silent jurisdictional clause.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: PROMESA § 106(a) directs that actions against the Oversight Board “shall be brought” in a U.S. district court, and in context that mandate functions as an affirmative authorization of suit rather than a mere venue clause, especially given Congress’s comprehensive supervisory design for Puerto Rico’s fiscal crisis under the Territory Clause. Although this Court’s clear-statement cases like Lane v. Peña and Sossamon v. Texas caution that jurisdictional/venue language alone is usually insufficient to waive or abrogate immunity, those cases address the ordinary federalism baseline; Puerto Rico’s territorial status and Congress’s plenary power lessen the structural concerns and counsel reading § 106(a) to ensure meaningful judicial oversight and access to remedies. Construing § 106(a) to preserve a sweeping immunity would practically insulate the Board from accountability, undermining access-to-justice interests and disproportionately harming the people of Puerto Rico, including those relying on transparency and territorial-law protections. Accordingly, I would hold that § 106(a), read in PROMESA’s remedial scheme, clearly authorizes suits against the Board in federal court for the claims at issue.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: PROMESA § 106(a), 48 U.S.C. § 2126(a), reads as a jurisdiction/forum-channeling provision—“any action against the Oversight Board … shall be brought” in the U.S. district court—without the kind of unequivocal waiver/abrogation language this Court requires to overcome sovereign immunity. Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: PROMESA § 106(a) is written as a venue/jurisdiction-channeling rule—actions against the Board “shall be brought” in a particular federal district court—not as an unequivocal waiver or abrogation of sovereign immunity. Lane v. Peña requires an “unequivocal expression” to alter immunity, and Sossamon v. Texas likewise rejects inferring consent to suit from general remedial or jurisdictional provisions. Respecting separation-of-powers and federalism-like immunity principles, I would not treat § 106(a)’s plain text as silently authorizing territorial-law disclosure claims against an immune entity.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: PROMESA § 106(a), 48 U.S.C. § 2126(a), is best read as a jurisdiction/venue-channeling provision specifying where suits against the Board must be filed if they are otherwise authorized; it does not mention sovereign immunity, waiver, or abrogation, and therefore does not satisfy this Court’s “unmistakably clear” clear-statement rule. Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: PROMESA § 106(a) is framed as a forum-direction provision—"shall be brought" in federal district court—without the sort of unequivocal textual signal this Court requires to conclude Congress meant to strip a sovereign entity of immunity. Under Atascadero State Hosp. v. Scanlon and Dellmuth v. Muth, abrogation must be "unmistakably clear" in the statutory text, and a grant of jurisdiction or venue-channeling alone does not suffice. Nothing in § 106(a) speaks in terms of "abrogation," "waiver," or "suits against the Board" notwithstanding immunity, so the separation-of-powers values served by the clear-statement rule counsel against inferring abrogation from implication or structural inferences. Whatever Congress may do under the Territory Clause, it must do so clearly, and § 106(a) does not meet that demand.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: PROMESA § 106(a), 48 U.S.C. § 2126(a), functions as a forum/jurisdiction-channeling provision (“shall be brought” in federal district court) and does not speak in unmistakably clear terms to abrogating sovereign immunity; under this Court’s clear-statement rule, Congress must make its intent to abrogate “unmistakably clear in the language of the statute.” Dellmuth v. Muth, 491 U.S. 223, 228 (1989). As in Atascadero and Sossamon, it is not enough to infer abrogation from general jurisdictional language or statutory structure when the text does not mention immunity, waiver, or amenability to suit. Respecting precedent and institutional stability counsels adhering to that demanding rule here, leaving any change to Congress to express clearly and directly.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: PROMESA § 106(a), 48 U.S.C. § 2126(a), is best read as a jurisdiction/venue-channeling provision—directing that any cognizable "action against the Oversight Board" must be filed in federal district court—rather than as an unequivocal elimination of an immunity defense. Under this Court’s clear-statement rule, Congress does not abrogate sovereign immunity absent text making that intent “unmistakably clear,” and statutory language that can naturally be understood as merely conferring jurisdiction does not suffice. See Dellmuth v. Muth, 491 U.S. 223, 228, 231–32 (1989) (no abrogation by “permissible inference”); Atascadero State Hosp. v. Scanlon, 473 U.S. 234, 242 (1985) (abrogation must be stated in the statute’s text with unmistakable clarity). Because § 106(a) does not mention immunity, waiver, or abrogation, it is susceptible to an interpretation consistent with retaining immunity, and thus fails the clear-statement requirement.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: PROMESA § 106(a), 48 U.S.C. § 2126(a), is framed as a forum-channeling/jurisdiction provision (“shall be brought” in district court) and does not speak in unmistakably clear terms to stripping the Board of any sovereign immunity defense. Under this Court’s clear-statement rule, Congress must make its intent to abrogate immunity “unmistakably clear in the language of the statute,” and courts may not infer abrogation from silence or structural implications. Atascadero State Hosp. v. Scanlon and Dellmuth v. Muth reject treating general jurisdictional grants as abrogation, and applying that rule here preserves procedural fairness and predictability by requiring Congress—not courts—to decide when to expose a sovereign entity to suit. Because § 106(a) lacks any express reference to immunity, waiver, or abrogation, it does not clearly abrogate whatever immunity the Board may otherwise possess.
